strengths: Extensive and carefully controlled experiments spanning multiple model families (Llama-3.1-8B/70B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen-2.5 7B-72B), multiple data sources (Goodfire SAE, Llama Scope SAE, Gemma Scope SAE, Wikipedia contrastive vectors), and multiple adapter architectures, with substantial appendix material supporting the main claims (training curves, PCA analysis, ablations, cross-family replication).

The core finding that a scalar affine adapter (d+1 parameters) captures ~85% of the benefit, and that this simple adapter generalizes better across datasets than higher-capacity alternatives, is a clean and useful empirical insight with a plausible mechanistic explanation (intrinsic dimensionality), supported by targeted controlled experiments (Appendix D) that rule out an alternative explanation (label count).

The application to decoding bridge entities in implicit multi-hop reasoning is a compelling and practically relevant use case, framed sensibly around alignment-auditing motivations, and shows a sizeable, well-quantified improvement over untrained self-interpretation.

The scaling analysis using a 'Taboo' baseline to separate self-interpretation gains from raw model capability gains is a thoughtful experimental design choice that strengthens the scaling claim beyond a naive 'bigger models are better at everything' story.

Reasonably transparent reporting of compute, hyperparameters, and dataset construction (including LLM prompts used for synthetic labeling), aiding reproducibility; code and adapters are stated to be released.

The ALL-CAPS and zero-vector probing experiments (Appendices I, J) provide a nice mechanistic decomposition of what the bias vector versus the input vector contribute, adding interpretability to the interpretability method itself.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is fairly simple (supervised regression/fine-tuning of a small affine map on frozen-model activation injection); most of the paper's value lies in the empirical characterization rather than a methodological advance, and no direct empirical comparison is made against the concurrent LoRA-based self-explanation approaches (LatentQA, Li et al. 2025, Karvonen et al. 2025) that are extensively discussed in related work.

Evaluation relies heavily on proxy metrics (generation scoring via latent activation on self-generated text, and embedding-based retrieval recall) rather than human judgment of interpretability quality or faithfulness; these metrics could reward fluent, plausible-sounding but ungrounded text if correlated with superficial lexical cues, and no human evaluation is reported.

The bridge-entity decoding results, while promising, are not fully ruled out as reflecting learned output-token priors/frequency biases rather than genuine extraction of latent semantic content from the residual stream; the paper acknowledges the adapter has a strong 'default interpretation prior' (bias vector) which raises the question of how much of the entity detection is prompt-consistent guessing versus genuine decoding of internal state.

The claim that 'self-interpretation improves with scale, outpacing capability gains' rests on a single family (Qwen) at only four scales and a single embedding-retrieval metric; the Taboo baseline, while a reasonable control, is itself confounded by task difficulty differences (paraphrase avoidance vs. direct naming) that may not cleanly isolate the intended capability-vs-interpretation distinction.

The explanation for why full-rank adapters overfit on SAE data but not on Wikipedia data (intrinsic dimensionality) is supported only by correlational PCA evidence and two controlled experiments, not a fully causal or theoretical account; alternative explanations (e.g., differences in training objective landscape, dataset size relative to feature diversity) are not fully excluded.

Some claims are stated with strong rhetorical force (e.g., 'trained adapters generate SAE feature labels that outperform the training labels themselves') that, while numerically supported by the specific hit-rate/coverage metrics used, may overstate generality given the narrowness of the evaluation protocol (generation scoring using the same underlying LM that also generated the labels being judged, raising potential for shared biases between generator and evaluator).

strengths: The paper is exceptionally thorough experimentally: it covers multiple model families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen), scales (7B–72B), and two distinct interpretability artifact sources (SAE features, contrastive vectors), with extensive ablations in the appendices (PCA/intrinsic dimensionality analysis, cross-layer generalization, ALL-CAPS probe, zero-vector bias analysis, data-scaling curves, shuffling controls).

The core architectural finding—that a scalar affine transform (d+1 parameters) captures ~85% of the achievable gain, and that full-rank adapters overfit catastrophically on high-dimensional SAE data but not on low-dimensional contrastive vectors—is a clean, mechanistically interesting result with a plausible dimensionality-based explanation supported by controlled experiments (Appendix D).

The bridge-entity/implicit-reasoning experiment (Section 3.5) is a compelling and relatively novel application, showing that trained adapters can surface latent intermediate reasoning (e.g., 'Plato') that never appears in the model's verbalized output, which is practically relevant to alignment auditing.

The method is lightweight and frozen-model, which is a meaningful design point relative to concurrent LoRA/full fine-tuning approaches (LatentQA, Li et al. 2025, Karvonen et al. 2025), preserving 'privileged access' arguments cleanly.
Reproducibility is reasonably well supported: detailed hyperparameters, dataset construction prompts, and compute accounting are all reported.
weaknesses: The headline claim that trained adapters 'outperform the training labels themselves' (71% vs 63%, and generally across Table 2/3) rests entirely on generation scoring, a metric that only checks whether generated text activates the latent and says nothing about specificity/precision (a broad, generic description can trivially inflate hit rate). Tellingly, the paper's own detection-F1 metric (Table 2), which is closer to a precision-recall style evaluation, shows the opposite ordering: auto-interpretability labels achieve the highest detection score (0.821), slightly above trained adapters (0.794-0.774). This directly undercuts the paper's central, most-advertised claim and is not adequately reconciled or caveated in the abstract/main text.

Generation scoring itself is potentially gameable: the adapter is trained on the very labels it is later claimed to 'outperform,' so improvements could partly reflect the adapter learning to produce broader/more activatable (but less specific) descriptions rather than more faithful ones. No precision-style analysis (e.g., false-positive rate, specificity across near-miss features) is offered to rule this out.

The 'self-interpretation scales with model size' claim (Section 3.3/Fig. 2) is built on a Taboo-baseline comparison using off-the-shelf embedding retrieval; the causal story that the narrowing gap reflects genuinely improved self-interpretive access (rather than, e.g., better instruction-following/verbosity at larger scale improving embedding retrieval scores generically) is not rigorously isolated. The single best-layer analysis (Fig. 15) even shows a non-monotonic anomaly at 32B, undermining the clean scaling story presented in the main text.

No direct empirical comparison against the concurrent fine-tuning-based approaches (LatentQA, Li et al. 2025, Karvonen et al. 2025) on shared benchmarks is provided; all comparisons to that line of work are qualitative/narrative in the Related Work and Discussion sections, weakening the significance claim that the frozen-adapter approach offers a superior trade-off.

Circularity concerns: detection scoring and generation scoring both rely on the same subject/interpreter LLM (as judge, as label-generator, and as the model being probed), which could introduce shared biases that inflate apparent self-interpretation quality without external validation (e.g., human evaluation of label quality is entirely absent).

The technical novelty is modest: the method is essentially a lightweight learned affine reparameterization layered onto the existing Patchscopes/SelfIE framework, closely analogous to prompt-tuning/soft-prompts and Tuned Lens; the main contribution is empirical characterization rather than a new mechanism, which is a legitimate contribution but is oversold in places (e.g., speculative 'RL from internal rewards' framing in the Discussion is asserted with more confidence than the evidence supports).

strengths: Extensive and carefully controlled empirical study spanning three model families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen), scales from 7B to 72B, and three distinct data sources (Goodfire SAEs, Llama/Gemma Scope SAEs, and a newly constructed Wikipedia contrastive-vector dataset), lending good external validity to the central claims.

The core finding that a minimal scalar affine adapter (d+1 parameters) captures ~85% of the achievable improvement, while full-rank adapters catastrophically overfit on SAE data but not on low-intrinsic-dimensionality Wikipedia vectors, is a genuinely interesting and well-supported mechanistic insight, backed by PCA analysis and controlled experiments isolating intrinsic dimensionality from label-count confounds (Appendix D).

The 'Taboo' baseline is a thoughtful control that isolates self-interpretation gains from raw capability gains across scale, strengthening the claim that self-interpretation quality scales favorably and non-trivially with model size.

The multi-hop reasoning / bridge-entity experiment is a compelling and novel application, showing the method generalizes from monosemantic training vectors to polysemantic residual-stream activations, with a large and clearly quantified improvement over untrained SelfIE.

Very strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, prompts, dataset construction pipeline, and compute accounting are all provided, and results are validated with SEMs and significance tests in the main tables.

The zero-vector and ALL-CAPS probing experiments (Appendices I, J) provide genuinely useful mechanistic insight into what the bias vector versus the input vector each contribute, going beyond a pure benchmark paper.
weaknesses: No direct empirical comparison against the decoder-finetuning alternatives (LatentQA, Li et al. 2025, Karvonen et al. 2025) that are discussed extensively as 'concurrent work'; the central positioning claim (frozen adapters vs. fine-tuning trade-off) is argued conceptually but not tested head-to-head on a shared task/dataset.

The generation-scoring and embedding-retrieval metrics are indirect proxies for interpretability quality (reactivation of a latent, or nearest-neighbor match in embedding space) rather than direct human judgments of description correctness; no human evaluation is included to corroborate the qualitative examples.

The best-of-6 protocol, while applied equally to baselines, still relies on a calibration step to select the scale grid per dataset/method, which could partially inflate reported gains and makes exact reproduction of the 'multi-scale' numbers somewhat dependent on this calibration procedure.

Because scalar affine adapters only apply a uniform scale and additive bias while preserving direction, and the bias vector accounts for the large majority of the improvement, it is unclear how much genuine per-vector (i.e., direction-specific) information is actually being read out versus how much of the gain reflects the adapter learning a better generic prior/target distribution for the self-interpretation task.

The Wikipedia contrastive-vector dataset (both training labels and part of the evaluation pipeline) is constructed and filtered using an LLM (Claude), and evaluated via another off-the-shelf embedding model; this introduces potential circularity/leakage concerns between data construction and evaluation that are not fully addressed.

The scaling analysis (Section 3.3) rests on only four model sizes within one model family (Qwen-2.5), and the appendix shows a non-monotonic trend at the single-layer level (32B underperforming 14B), suggesting the 'scaling law' claim is somewhat sensitive to methodological choices (layer pooling vs. single-layer evaluation).

The paper's framing of adapters 'outperforming training labels themselves' is an interesting result but is somewhat expected for any model that aggregates structure across thousands of noisy labels (akin to denoising by regression); the framing could be tempered or more precisely contextualized relative to this expectation.

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical investigation: adapter architecture comparisons (identity, scale-only, scalar affine, low-rank, full-rank), replicated across three model families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen) and multiple scales (7B-72B), with consistent findings, greatly strengthening the reliability of the central claims.

Genuinely interesting and non-obvious findings well-supported by controlled ablations: (1) the bias vector alone explains ~85% of improvement, verified via zero-vector probing (Appendix J) and ALL-CAPS format-transfer experiments (Appendix I) that cleanly separate 'format/prior' from 'semantic content'; (2) full-rank adapters overfit catastrophically on SAE data but not on Wikipedia contrastive vectors, and the paper rules out the label-count confound via a well-designed controlled experiment (Appendix D.2), isolating intrinsic dimensionality as the causal factor.

Careful, self-critical evaluation methodology: a two-phase select-then-rescore protocol explicitly designed to eliminate selection-on-noise bias (Appendix A.5), use of two complementary SAE metrics (detection vs. generation scoring) with an honest discussion of when/why they disagree (Appendix K), and comparisons against strong baselines including LoRA-based Activation Oracles and linear probes.

The bridge-entity/implicit multi-hop reasoning application (Section 3.6) is a compelling and novel demonstration that trained adapters generalize from monosemantic training vectors to polysemantic residual-stream activations, with a meaningful practical framing (surfacing unverbalized reasoning for alignment auditing).

Strong attention to reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, compute budgets, dataset construction prompts, and extensive appendix material (26 pages) covering training dynamics, cross-layer/cross-family generalization, and data-scaling curves.

The scaling analysis with a capability-controlled 'Taboo' baseline is a thoughtful design choice that isolates self-interpretation gains from raw model capability gains, addressing an obvious confound.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution (learning an affine/low-rank mapping from activations into token-embedding space) is technically simple; the paper's primary value is empirical characterization rather than a new interpretability method, which may be seen as an incremental contribution relative to Patchscopes/SelfIE.

Evaluation heavily depends on LLM-based judges and LLM-generated synthetic data: auto-interpretability labels, generation-scoring contexts, detection-scoring judges, and even the Wikipedia training labels are all produced or validated by other LLMs (including the same model family being evaluated). This raises concerns about circularity and about whether 'outperforming training labels' partly reflects LLM-judge idiosyncrasies rather than genuine semantic improvement.

Headline abstract numbers (e.g., 94% recall@1, 70% vs 50% generation scoring) are obtained with best-of-N candidate selection and scale tuning, while some in-text results (e.g., 82.9% recall@1 in Section 3.2) are reported without these aids; the abstract does not clearly flag this distinction, which could mislead readers about the 'default' performance of the method.

Practical deployability is limited by the need for a scale-selection procedure at inference (grid search over ~6-12 scales per vector); the paper does not propose or evaluate a principled/automatic way to pick the scale, which is central to the method's reliability claims.

For the bridge-entity task, while aggregate detection rates are high (91%), the per-generation reliability is still fairly low (4.26% of individual generations contain the entity even in successful cases), suggesting the signal, while statistically detectable in aggregate, may be too noisy for direct practical auditing use without further development.

The paper's discussion of 'privileged access' and self-interpretation superiority is largely qualitative; no direct experiment compares whether the *same* model's adapter genuinely outperforms an *identical* adapter trained to have a different model interpret this model's activations (i.e., isolating whether privileged self-access, versus just having a good learned mapian function, drives the results).

The manuscript is extremely dense, with the 9-page main text relying substantially on a very long appendix (26 pages) for core supporting evidence (e.g., the dimensionality/overfitting analysis, cross-family results, and metric disagreement analysis), which may hinder accessibility and self-containedness of the main submission.

strengths: Extensive empirical scope: experiments span three distinct interpretability artifact datasets (Goodfire SAE, Llama Scope SAE, Wikipedia contrastive vectors), multiple model families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen), and scales from 7B to 72B/70B, with replication of key findings across families in appendices.

Careful methodological hygiene in places: the two-phase select-then-rescore protocol (Appendix A.5) explicitly addresses selection-on-noise bias that would otherwise inflate best-of-N comparisons, and SEMs/paired t-tests are reported throughout.

Useful ablation isolating the bias vector's contribution (85% of the gain) and a well-controlled dimensionality analysis (Appendix D.2) that rules out label-count as a confound for why full-rank adapters overfit on SAE data but not on Wikipedia topic vectors.

The bridge-entity decoding experiment (Section 3.6) is a genuinely interesting application, showing the approach can surface latent intermediate reasoning not present in the prompt or response, with a reasonable comparison against linear probes.
Comparison against a relevant fine-tuning baseline (LoRA-based Activation Oracles) and against untrained SelfIE, situating the contribution within the current self-interpretation literature.
weaknesses: Central soundness concern: generation scoring and detection scoring both use the same frozen subject model (as generator and/or judge) that is also the model being interpreted and the model whose adapter is being trained. This creates a correlated/self-referential evaluation loop that could inflate the apparent advantage of trained adapters over baselines (e.g., auto-interp labels produced by a different pipeline) without necessarily reflecting more faithful interpretation; this concern is not discussed or controlled for.

The headline claim that adapters 'outperform the training labels themselves' holds only under generation scoring, not detection scoring (where the trained adapter ties but does not exceed the strongest baseline, Table 2/3) — the abstract and framing emphasize the more favorable metric without adequately foregrounding this discrepancy for a general audience.

The scaling experiment (Figure 2, Section 3.5) uses full-rank adapters whose parameter count grows as d_model^2, so adapter capacity scales super-linearly with model size; this is a plausible confound for the 'self-interpretation improves with scale' claim that is not addressed or ablated against a fixed-capacity adapter across scales.

No human evaluation of generated interpretations anywhere in the paper — all quality assessment is automated (embedding retrieval, generation/detection scoring by the same model family), which is a significant gap for a paper centrally about whether models can faithfully describe their internal states.

The core technical contribution (a scalar/low-rank affine map trained via cross-entropy on vector-label pairs, injected as a soft token) is conceptually modest and closely related to existing soft-prompt/prefix-tuning and Tuned-Lens-style approaches; the paper's framing in terms of 'self-interpretation,' 'privileged access,' and speculative extensions ('RL from internal rewards,' 'catching models red-handed') arguably oversells the significance relative to what is technically a lightweight learned linear probe/decoder.

Absolute performance on the harder, more realistic polysemantic setting (bridge-entity detection) remains low in absolute terms (≈4% of generations contain the entity even for successful cases), raising questions about practical utility despite large relative improvements over the untrained baseline.

Key reproducibility detail (the published link to the Wikipedia topics dataset) is missing/blank in the text, and the dataset construction pipeline relies on a proprietary LLM (Claude Sonnet) with substantial manual curation/filtering choices that may be hard for others to exactly replicate.

The explanation for why full-rank works on Wikipedia vectors but not SAE features (intrinsic dimensionality) is plausible but remains a post-hoc empirical correlation rather than a theoretically grounded account, and it is not clear how predictive this heuristic would be for new artifact types.

strengths: Extensive, carefully controlled experimental suite spanning multiple model families (Llama-3.1-8B/3.3-70B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen-2.5 7B-72B) and two distinct representation classes (SAE decoder vectors, contrastive activation vectors), with consistent replication of core findings across settings (Appendices G, F).

Methodologically rigorous evaluation protocol: the two-phase select-then-rescore procedure (Appendix A.5) explicitly addresses selection-on-noise bias that would otherwise inflate best-of-N comparisons, and is applied consistently and transparently.

Genuinely informative ablations that explain *why* results hold, not just that they hold: the PCA/intrinsic-dimensionality analysis (Section 3.3, Appendix D) convincingly explains why full-rank adapters overfit on SAE features but not contrastive vectors, and controlled experiments rule out label-count as a confound.

The decomposition of adapter behavior into a bias term (format/prior) and scale-dependent input contribution (semantics) is well supported by targeted experiments (ALL-CAPS training in Appendix I, zero-vector probing in Appendix J), giving real mechanistic insight into what the adapter learns.

The bridge-entity/implicit-reasoning application (Section 3.6) is a compelling, non-trivial demonstration of practical utility beyond toy settings, including a fair comparison against trained linear probes and SAE-trained adapters as controls.

Honest and detailed treatment of limitations and nuances, including the divergence between detection and generation scoring (Appendix K) and candid acknowledgment that self-interpretation does not guarantee faithfulness or safety coverage (Impact Statement).
Good reproducibility: hyperparameters, compute budgets, prompts, and dataset construction procedures are documented in substantial detail.
weaknesses: The evaluation metrics (generation scoring, detection scoring, embedding retrieval) are behavioral proxies that test whether a label can reproduce or discriminate activating contexts via the same frozen model, not independent verification of semantic faithfulness; an adapter could learn surface regularities that satisfy these benchmarks without genuinely 'introspecting.' This concern is acknowledged only partially in the Discussion.

Claims that adapters 'outperform the training labels themselves' could partly reflect a denoising/regression-to-the-mean effect from aggregating over many noisy single labels rather than a qualitatively new interpretive capability; the paper's own analogy to regression supports this alternative but less novel explanation.

Practical deployment requires a best-of-N scale sweep with no principled way to select the correct scale without ground truth, which is a meaningful limitation for real-world auditing use cases (the paper reports results under this best-of-N regime as if it were close to a deployed system in several places).

The absolute rates for the bridge-entity detection task are modest in the single-generation setting (e.g., 4.26% of individual generations contain the entity for the trained adapter), and the much more impressive aggregate numbers (91% of prompts detected) are computed by pooling over many layers, positions, and samples, which may overstate practical utility for a single auditing query.

The core technical contribution (an affine or low-rank affine map trained with cross-entropy on vector-label pairs) is simple, and much of the paper's novelty rests on empirical characterization rather than a new algorithmic idea; this is defensible but somewhat limits originality.

Significant methodological detail (e.g., the two-phase scoring protocol, which is central to the validity of the headline comparisons) is relegated to the appendix, and the extensive appendix material, while valuable, makes it harder to assess at a glance which findings are central versus incidental.

The forward-looking 'RL from internal rewards' discussion is speculative with no accompanying experiments, and the overall framing in the abstract ('self-interpretation improves with scale') may be stronger than the underlying taboo-baseline-controlled evidence, which is limited to one dataset (Wikipedia topics) and one architecture (full-rank affine) at scale.
